result:
There is a particular quality of light in late September that I have never been able to name. It hangs in the air like dust motes suspended in a sunbeam, golden but not warm, bright but not harsh. It is the light that makes you notice the ordinary—the way a spiderweb catches dew on the fence, the way a leaf detaches itself from a branch and takes its time falling, as if undecided. I have been thinking about that light all day, and about how much of our lives are spent in the company of things we fail to notice until they are almost gone.

I remember a morning, years ago, when I woke early and went to the kitchen to make coffee. The house was quiet in that particular way that only exists before anyone else is awake. The refrigerator hummed. A bird, unseen, repeated the same three notes over and over. And there, on the windowsill, was a glass of water I had left the night before. The light came through it in a way that seemed impossible, splitting into a small rainbow that fell across the counter. I stood there watching it for longer than I should have. It was nothing, really. Just water and glass and sun. But I have carried that moment with me for a decade, and I cannot tell you why.

That is the thing about being alive. The moments that stay with you are never the ones you plan for. They are the accidents, the in-between places, the seconds that pass while you are waiting for something else to happen. You remember the time you missed the train, and the stranger who nodded at you on the platform. You remember the smell of rain on hot pavement, the sound of your own footsteps in an empty hallway, the way a song you had forgotten suddenly comes back to you in full, like a door opening.

I have been thinking about time, too. Not in the abstract, but in the way it behaves when you are not paying attention. There is a theory that time is not a river but a series of moments, each one discrete, like frames in a film. If that is true, then our lives are not continuous at all. They are a flickering sequence of stills, and what we call memory is just the brain's way of stitching them together into a story. I like this idea. It explains why certain moments feel so vivid, so preserved, as if they were dipped in amber. They are not part of the flow. They are the film itself.

I think of my grandmother, who lived to be ninety-two, and who spent her last years in a small room that smelled of lavender and old paper. She had a habit of telling the same stories over and over, and I would sometimes grow impatient. But now I understand. She was not repeating herself. She was revisiting the moments that mattered, polishing them like stones, keeping them alive. She told me once that the secret to a good life was not to do great things but to notice small ones. I was sixteen. I thought she meant that I should appreciate sunsets and wildflowers. But I know better now. She meant that the great things are usually invisible. They are the cups of tea, the folded laundry, the hand on a shoulder, the patient listening.

There is a word in Japanese—*mono no aware*—that has no direct English equivalent. It means, roughly, the bittersweet awareness of impermanence, the gentle sadness that comes from knowing that all things will pass. I have been thinking about that word. It is not a melancholy word, exactly. It is more like a kind of tenderness. It is the feeling you get when you see cherry blossoms falling, or when you watch a friend drive away, or when you finish a good book and sit for a moment with the closed cover in your hands. It is the acknowledgment that beauty is fleeting, and that this is precisely what makes it beautiful.

I have a photograph of a beach I visited once, in a country I have never returned to. The photograph is not particularly good. The horizon is crooked, and a stranger's umbrella intrudes on the edge of the frame. But every time I look at it, I am there again. I can feel the sand under my feet, the salt on my lips, the specific weight of the day. And I wonder if that is what we are doing when we write, when we tell stories, when we paint or sing. We are trying to hold onto the moments that would otherwise dissolve. We are trying to make the falling leaf pause, just for a second.

I have been writing for most of my life, and I still do not fully understand why. It is not for fame, which I have never had. It is not for money, which I have never made. It is, I think, for the same reason that my grandmother told her stories. It is to keep things. To preserve them. To make a record of the light in September, the glass of water on the windowsill, the sound of a bird repeating three notes. Writing is a way of saying: this happened, and it mattered, and I will not let it be forgotten.

There is a danger, of course, in living too much in the past. I know that. The present is where we actually are. The present is where the coffee is hot and the people we love are still here. But I think there is also a danger in living too much in the present, in letting every moment slip through your fingers untended. We need both. We need to be here, now, fully awake. And we need to carry with us the things we have seen, so that we can understand what we are seeing now.

I am sitting at my desk as I write this. The light outside has changed. It is later now, the golden hour gone, replaced by the blue-gray of evening. The spiderweb on the fence is invisible again. The bird has stopped singing. Soon it will be dark, and then it will be tomorrow, and the light will come back, different, never quite the same. That is the deal. That is the arrangement we have made with time. We get to see things, but only once. We get to hold them, but only for a moment.

So here is what I want to say. Notice. Notice the small things, the ordinary things, the things that seem too insignificant to matter. Notice the way your child's hand fits in yours. Notice the first sip of coffee in the morning. Notice the crack in the sidewalk where a dandelion has pushed through. Notice the sound of rain on the roof at 3 a.m. Notice the person who lets you merge in traffic. Notice the way the light comes through a glass of water. It will not come again, not like that, not ever. And someday, you will want it back.

That is all I have to say. It is not much. But it is true, and it is everything.
